layman_trigger: Scanlon's test skips your suffering sums: an act is wrong only if principles no one could reasonably reject forbid it. Judged by the prospects they offer, a principle permitting procreation in decent conditions gives the created a bet no rational agent would refuse — the same hypothetical consent that licenses surgery on the unconscious. So procreation clears a serious, standalone ethics.
layman_gloss: Runs on justifying creation to a standpoint judged by its prospects. The reply: that standpoint has no occupant — every consent analogy pays someone who already exists.
layman_win_line: Hypothetical consent needs a bearer — creation manufactures its subject only afterward.
layman_diagnosis: Grant the strongest form — prospects, not outcomes; hypothetical consent as ordinary moral currency. But that currency pays someone who exists: patient before scalpel, ward before guardian, public before road. Creation manufactures its own subject — before it, no one faces the prospect; after it, only a done deal. Scanlon's point was justification to each, not the average; yet the child dealt the catastrophic life is told her complaint was priced into a standpoint she never occupied. Hypothetical consent works where refusal would also burden someone who exists; non-creation burdens no one. It keeps Scanlon's name and surrenders his point.
